title: Stick & Stone Maths
strapline: Counting, sorting and pattern-making with what the ground gives — maths in the mud, using nature's own loose parts.
intent: Children build number sense outdoors, counting, comparing and subitising with real, textured, freely available objects.
Children sort, classify and pattern with natural loose parts, making and explaining their own rules.
Children explore size, length, weight and measure by comparing sticks, stones, cones and leaves.
Children experience maths as playful, physical and everywhere — not confined to a table or a worksheet.
Children combine gross-motor outdoor play with mathematical thinking, learning through their whole body.
implementation: Gather rich collections of natural loose parts — sticks, stones, pine cones, conkers, shells, leaves — in baskets ready to count and sort.
Model counting with a touch per object and a fuss over the last number: 'one, two, three, FOUR stones!'
Set open sorting invitations — 'can you group these however you like?' — then ask children to explain their rule.
Compare and measure with real questions: 'which stick is longest? how many stones balance one big pebble?'
Make patterns with natural materials — stone, stick, stone, stick — and leave one unfinished for a child to continue.
Weave maths through outdoor play all day — counting steps, comparing puddles, sharing conkers fairly — so it's a habit, not a slot.
key_questions: How many stones do you think are in your pile — shall we count?
How did you decide which ones go together?
Which stick is the longest? How could we check?
What comes next in your stone pattern?
Have we enough conkers to share one each?

impact.text: Children count natural objects with one-to-one correspondence and know the last number is the answer.
Children subitise small amounts — seeing two or three stones without counting.
Children sort and classify by their own rule and explain it when asked.
Children copy, continue and create patterns with sticks and stones and talk about them.
Children compare length, size and weight using words like longer, heavier, more.

enhancements: Balance scales outdoors: how many acorns weigh the same as one big stone?
A number-hunt trail — find three of something, find five sticks longer than your hand.
Numeral pebbles children match to the right quantity of loose parts.
Big stick-and-stone patterns laid out on the ground for the whole group to continue.
A tallying game — collecting and grouping conkers into tens as they gather.

playing_exploring: Children handle beautiful natural collections because they want to — the maths follows the fascination.
Open-ended loose parts invite children to invent their own counting and sorting games.
active_learning: Checking a guess by counting — and being right — is a satisfaction children chase again.
Children persist to complete a long pattern or balance the scales exactly.
creating_thinking: Children spot and extend patterns and use them to predict what comes next.
They devise their own sorting rules and strategies and can explain their thinking.
